summary.text: A 50 year old, previously healthy man had a first episode of enuresis in early summer of 2008, then two to three additional episodes of nocturnal enuresis that always occurred in spring or summer, and consulted no one about it. He had no history of syncope, seizures, chest discomfort or nocturnal agonal respiration, and no family history of sudden cardiac death.

On the day of admission he awoke at 0340 h to a wet bed; at 0416 h his wife noticed him groaning and unresponsive and started basic life support. At 0436 h emergency medical technicians found ventricular fibrillation, and at 0447 h he was resuscitated after two defibrillations and epinephrine. He was transferred to the emergency department in September 2013.

At 0511 h, following hospital admission, he was unresponsive, with physical examination and laboratory results otherwise unremarkable. Coronary angiography showed normal coronary arteries and echocardiography showed no structural heart disease and normal ventricular function. The electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with transient coved-type ST elevation in V2 and saddleback type ST elevation on a different day, and Brugada syndrome was diagnosed.

He underwent therapeutic hypothermia, was extubated on the fourth hospital day without neurological deficit, and an implantable cardioverter defibrillator was inserted. His bed was dry during a night-time ventricular fibrillation episode treated by an ICD shock in May 2015, and at last follow-up in July 2016 he was in good condition.
